title: Fatima al-Fihri and the First University
summary: How Fatima al-Fihri used her inheritance to found al-Qarawiyyin in Fez in 859, and how it grew into a university that is still open today.
poll: One person's choice can still help people more than a thousand years later.

versions.title: A Gift That Still Helps
versions.text:
This is a true tale from long ago. A girl named Fatima lived in a town. Her dad sold things. He was rich.

They left home. They went far west. They went to a big city. It was Fez. Lots of new folks came to live there.

Then her dad died. She and her sister got his wealth. She had a plan. She would help the town.

It was the year 859. She paid to build a mosque. It was a place to pray. It was a place to learn, too.

Lots of men came to learn. Each one was a student. They read books. They learned math. They learned the stars. A big library held the books.

Now the school is a university. It is a school for grown-ups. It is still open! It is more than one thousand years old.

Fatima al-Fihri did not keep her wealth. She gave a gift. It was a place to learn. That gift still helps.

Fatima did not keep her wealth just for her. She gave a gift. It was a place to learn. That gift still helps us all.

versions.title: Fatima and Her School
versions.text:
Long ago, a girl named Fatima al-Fihri was born in a town called Kairouan. Her father was a trader. He bought and sold goods. He got rich.

When Fatima was young, her family moved far to the west. They made a new home in the city of Fez, in Morocco. Lots of folks from Kairouan lived there.

Then her father died. Fatima and her sister got his wealth. Fatima wanted to do good with it. She chose to help her new city.

In the year 859, Fatima paid to build a mosque. It was a place to pray. It was a place to learn, too. It was named Qarawiyyin, for the people from her old town.

Soon, lots of men came to learn there. Each student sat in a ring around a teacher. They read the Quran. They learned to read and write well. They learned math and how the stars move. A big library held their books.

Now the school is a university. It is still open, more than one thousand years later! Some say it is the oldest one in the world.

Fatima did not keep her wealth for herself. She built a place to learn. Her gift still helps people now.

More than a thousand years ago, a girl named Fatima al-Fihri was born in Kairouan, a city in what is now Tunisia. Her father, Mohammed, was a successful merchant who traded goods across North Africa, and his business made the family wealthy.

When Fatima was young, her family journeyed far to the west and settled in Fez, a growing city in Morocco. Many other families from Kairouan had also moved there, so the newcomers formed their own neighborhood on one side of the river.

After her father died, Fatima and her sister Mariam inherited his fortune. Instead of spending the money on themselves, both sisters decided to use it to benefit their community. Mariam built one mosque, and Fatima built another, larger one.

In the year 859, Fatima founded a mosque called al-Qarawiyyin, which she named after the people of her former home. It was built for prayer, but it soon became an important center of learning as well.

Students gathered in circles around a scholar, who taught them while they listened, asked questions, and took notes. They studied the Quran, the Arabic language, and law, and they also learned mathematics, medicine, and astronomy. Eventually, a large library was added, and people traveled from distant lands to gain knowledge there.

Today, al-Qarawiyyin is a university, and it remains open more than a thousand years after it began. Many experts describe it as the oldest existing university in the world that has continued teaching without closing.

Fatima could have kept her wealth for herself. Instead, she created a place of learning that has served students for centuries. Her story shows how one person's choice can make a difference for a very long time.

versions.title: Fatima al-Fihri and the First University
versions.text:
More than eleven centuries ago, a girl named Fatima al-Fihri was born in Kairouan, a city in what is now Tunisia. Her father, Mohammed, was a successful merchant who traded goods across North Africa, and his business made the family rich. Historians know little else about her early life, because most of the records that describe her were written long after she died.

When Fatima was young, her family moved west and settled in Fez, a growing city in Morocco, where many other families from Kairouan had already set up their own neighborhood.

After her father's death, Fatima and her sister Mariam inherited his large fortune. Rather than spending the money on themselves, the generous sisters decided to invest it in their community. Mariam built one mosque, and Fatima built another, even larger one.

In the year 859, Fatima founded a mosque called al-Qarawiyyin, naming it after the people of her former home. Although it was built for prayer, it slowly grew into an important institution of learning.

Students gathered in circles around respected scholars, listening carefully, asking questions, and taking notes. They studied the Quran, Arabic grammar, and law, alongside mathematics, medicine, and astronomy. Eventually, a grand library was added, which came to hold precious handwritten manuscripts, and scholars traveled from distant lands to share knowledge there.

Today, al-Qarawiyyin is a university, and it is still open more than a thousand years after it began. Many experts recognize it as the oldest existing university in the world that has kept teaching without a break.

In 1963, al-Qarawiyyin became part of Morocco's modern university system. Its famous library, which holds very old handwritten manuscripts, was also carefully repaired and reopened in 2016, so that students and researchers could use it again.

Why does this story still matter? In Fatima's time, few people could read, and every book had to be copied by hand, one page at a time, so a place where anyone who wanted to learn could sit with a good teacher was a rare and valuable gift.

Fatima's legacy is therefore remarkable. She could easily have kept her wealth for herself, but instead she created a place of learning that has served students for centuries.

More than eleven centuries ago, a girl named Fatima al-Fihri was born in Kairouan, a city located in present-day Tunisia. Her father, Mohammed, was a successful merchant who traded goods across North Africa, and his business made the family prosperous. Historians know relatively little else about her early life, because most of the surviving descriptions of her were written several centuries after her death.

During Fatima's childhood, her family journeyed westward and settled in Fez, an expanding city in Morocco, where numerous other families from Kairouan had already established a neighborhood of their own.

After her father's death, Fatima and her sister Mariam inherited his considerable fortune. Rather than spending the money on personal comforts, the generous sisters decided to invest it in their community. Mariam constructed one mosque, and Fatima constructed another, even larger one.

In the year 859, Fatima founded a mosque called al-Qarawiyyin, naming it in honor of the people of her former home. Although it was originally intended for prayer, it gradually developed into a respected institution of education.

Students gathered in circles around distinguished scholars, listening attentively, asking questions, and recording notes. They studied the Quran, Arabic grammar, and law, alongside mathematics, medicine, and astronomy. Eventually, a magnificent library was added, which came to preserve precious handwritten manuscripts, and scholars traveled from distant regions to exchange knowledge there.

Today, al-Qarawiyyin operates as a university, and it remains open more than a thousand years after its founding. Organizations such as UNESCO recognize it as the oldest existing educational institution in the world that has continued teaching without interruption.

In 1963, al-Qarawiyyin became part of Morocco's modern university system. Its famous library, which holds very old handwritten manuscripts, was also carefully repaired and reopened in 2016, so that students and researchers could use it again.

Why does this story still matter today? In Fatima's time, few people could read, and every book had to be copied by hand, one page at a time, so a place where anyone who wanted to learn could sit with a good teacher was a rare and valuable gift. Her choice reminds us that one person who shares what she has can change the lives of people she will never meet.

Fatima's legacy is therefore remarkable. She could easily have kept her inheritance for herself, but instead she created a place of learning that has served generations of students.

HIGH.prompt: The author says Fatima's legacy is remarkable. Do you agree? Support your answer with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.

HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that Fatima's legacy is remarkable, because she turned a personal inheritance into an institution that has lasted over a thousand years. Instead of keeping her father's wealth for herself, she made the generous choice to found al-Qarawiyyin, a place where students could study subjects ranging from law to the movement of the stars. That mosque eventually became a university that historians still call the oldest in the world to have never closed, which means her gift is still changing lives today. Few people's choices echo across so many centuries, which is exactly why her legacy deserves to be called remarkable.
